headings.text: 3 A system with friction: block on a table and hanging block

html:
The big picture

The lecture turns the recipe of 8 Newton's Laws and Forces into a method and adds the force that resists motion. A free-body diagram cuts a system (here a block on a table, joined by a rope over a pulley to a hanging block) into its parts and draws, for each part separately, every force acting on it: a cut rope becomes its rope force F_R, a cut contact the normal force F_N (and friction). Each part then gives one equation \sum F = m a per direction. Friction comes in several types: static friction holds a body at rest, up to \mu_S F_N; sliding friction \mu_D F_N acts on a moving body, with \mu_S \ge \mu_D; rolling friction \mu_W F_N acts on a rolling wheel and is much smaller. The friction coefficient \mu belongs to a pair of materials, and \mu > 1 is possible. The block-and-pulley system combines everything, written with inertial forces m\cdot a (d'Alembert) so that each part is "in balance". Moving through a fluid gives speed-dependent friction: liquid friction \propto v, air friction \propto v^2. Rope friction around a cylinder grows exponentially with the wrap angle.

Organisation (23 Oct, board): no class today at 13:30. Tutoring starts next week: Thursdays 18:00–19:30 and Fridays 13:30–15:00, starting Oct 29/30.

1 Free-body diagrams

Lecture: p. 7 ("Re-cap", "Free body diagrams") · Giancoli §4-7

\sum_i \vec F_i = m\vec a holds for one body and counts only the forces on that body. A system of several bodies is therefore cut apart, and each part is drawn on its own with all forces acting on it: a free-body diagram. Wherever you cut, you replace what was cut by the force it exerted:

  • a cut rope by its pull F_R, along the rope, away from the body (a rope can only pull);
  • a cut contact surface by the normal force F_N, perpendicular to the surface, pushing into the body (with friction, also a friction force along it, section 2);
  • and every body keeps its weight F_G.

By the reaction principle, the two sides of each cut carry equal and opposite forces.

The first version (p. 7, without friction), part by part:

  • I (block m_1): F_{G1} down, F_{N1} up (the table pushes), F_R to the right (the rope pulls).
  • II (block m_2): F_R up, F_{G2} down.
  • III (pulley): rope forces F_R to the left and F_R down; "NO FRICTION". The rope runs over the pulley, so it pulls on it along both segments. The axle's holding force isn't drawn, because nothing in the problem needs it.
  • IV (table): an arrow F_{G1} (up) and F_{N1} (down).

"TO BE CONTINUED …"

Symbols
  • F_{G1} = m_1 g, F_{G2} = m_2 g — weights of the two blocks (N)
  • F_{N1} — normal force between table and block 1 (N)
  • F_R — rope force (tension) (N), R for "rope"
  • I–IV — the four parts the system is cut into

The same F_R appears at I, II and III because of two idealisations: an ideal rope (massless, not stretching) and a pulley with "no friction". Then the pulley only redirects the rope's pull; the tension is the same along the whole rope.

Unclear (p. 7 / p. 9): the forces drawn on the table (IV)

On IV the board draws an upward arrow labelled F_{G1} and a downward arrow labelled F_{N1}. On the table itself, the block's contribution is one downward push: the reaction to F_{N1} (F'_{N1} in the notation of 8 Newton's Laws and Forces, equal in size to F_{N1}). F_{G1} acts on the block, not on the table. The sketch is probably meant as "the pair across the cut". IV isn't used in the equations that follow.

Problem-solving steps — free-body diagrams
  1. Sketch the system and mark every cut: ropes, contact surfaces.
  2. Draw each body separately. Forces on it: its weight; at each cut rope a pull along the rope; at each contact a normal force (and friction, against the sliding or the tendency to slide).
  3. Draw only forces on that body; label each by its source.
  4. Choose axes per body (along the motion is convenient) and write \sum F = m a per direction.
  5. Link the bodies: same rope tension (ideal rope and pulley), same size of acceleration (rope doesn't stretch), reaction pairs equal and opposite.
  6. Count unknowns and equations; solve; check limiting cases.

2 Friction: sliding and static

Lecture: p. 7–8 ("Friction", "Types of friction") and p. 9 ("Some friction values") · Giancoli §5-1

When two surfaces touch, a force along the contact resists their sliding against each other: friction. It is described by a friction coefficient, the "GREEK LETTER 'MU'", \mu: a pure number that belongs to a pair of materials (steel on steel, rubber on asphalt).

Sliding friction (\to \mu_K \to \mu_G) acts once the surfaces move against each other:

F_F = \mu_D\cdot F_N

with "↑ DYNAMIC FRICTION COEFF."

Symbols
  • F_F — friction force on the sliding body (N), opposite to its velocity relative to the surface
  • \mu_D — the dynamic friction coefficient (dimensionless)
  • F_N — the normal force (N): how hard the surfaces are pressed together, perpendicular to them

\mu_K ("kinetic", English textbooks) and \mu_G (German Gleitreibung) are other names for the same coefficient. Sliding friction has a fixed size, \mu_D F_N, and points against the sliding. Pressing the surfaces together harder makes them grip harder, in proportion; the friction force is nearly independent of the contact area and of the speed.

Static friction acts between surfaces that do not slide relative to each other; it holds a parked car on a slope or a crate you push but can't move:

F_F = \mu_S\cdot F_N

with "↑ STATIC FRICTION COEFF." under \mu_S and "← NORMAL FORCE" at F_N.

Symbols
  • F_F — static friction force (N), along the contact surface
  • \mu_S — the static friction coefficient (dimensionless)
  • F_N — the normal force (N)

What the board writes is the largest static friction the contact can supply. Up to that limit, static friction is exactly as large as needed to stop sliding: push a heavy crate with 10 N and friction answers with 10 N; push with 50 N and it answers with 50 N. Precisely:

F_F \le \mu_S\,F_N \quad\text{(static)}, \qquad F_F = \mu_S\,F_N \quad\text{only at the limit, just before it slips}

Symbols as above. The board's box:

\boxed{\,\mu_S \ge \mu_D\,}
Symbols
  • \mu_S, \mu_D — static and dynamic friction coefficient of the same pair of surfaces

It is harder to start a body sliding than to keep it sliding.

Why is \mu_S \ge \mu_D?

At rest the two surfaces have time to settle into each other: the microscopic bumps interlock and small contact spots bond. To start sliding, all of these must be broken at once. Once the body slides, the bumps skip over each other and have no time to settle, so less force is needed. Hence the jolt when an object "breaks free", and the stick–slip judder of a squeaking door.

Worked example — does the crate move?

A 30 kg crate on a floor, \mu_S = 0.5, \mu_D = 0.3; you push horizontally with 100 N.

  1. Normal force: the floor carries the weight (no vertical acceleration), F_N = mg = 30 \cdot 9.81 \approx 294\,\mathrm N.
  2. Maximum static friction: \mu_S F_N \approx 0.5 \cdot 294 \approx 147\,\mathrm N. Your 100 N is less, so the crate stays put, and static friction is exactly 100\,\mathrm N (not 147 N).
  3. Push just over 147 N and it breaks free; then keep it sliding: sliding friction is \mu_D F_N \approx 88\,\mathrm N, so about 88 N keeps it moving at constant speed.

Extremes and a myth (board): "IF \mu = 0; \mu = \infty 'INFINITE'" and "MYTH \mu = 1 / \mu > 1 — 'URBAN LEGEND'". \mu = 0 is a perfectly smooth contact, an idealisation like ice in textbook problems; \mu = \infty would mean fully stuck. Real pairs lie in between. The urban legend is that a friction coefficient can't exceed 1, as if friction could never exceed the normal force. Nothing in F_F = \mu F_N forbids \mu > 1; it only means the surfaces grip very strongly. Soft rubber on dry asphalt, racing tyres or very clean metal surfaces exceed 1, which is how a racing car can brake at more than 1\,g.

On a slope. Board sketch (p. 8): a block on a slope of 45^\circ, with "← STICKS AT 45° WHEN \mu = 1". The board states it without the calculation. For a block of mass m on a slope with angle \theta:

  1. The weight mg points straight down; the angle between it and the slope's normal is also \theta. So the part pressing into the slope is mg\cos\theta, the part pulling down along it mg\sin\theta (check: on flat ground, \theta = 0, nothing pulls along ✓).
  2. Perpendicular to the slope nothing accelerates, so F_N = mg\cos\theta.
  3. The block sticks while the pull along the slope does not exceed the largest static friction:
mg\sin\theta \le \mu_S\,F_N = \mu_S\,mg\cos\theta \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \tan\theta \le \mu_S
Symbols
  • \theta — slope angle; \tan\theta = \sin\theta/\cos\theta; other symbols as above

(Divide both sides by mg\cos\theta > 0; the mass cancels.) At 45^\circ, \tan 45^\circ = 1, so the block just sticks when \mu_S = 1: the board's sketch. This is also how \mu_S is measured: tilt until it slides, then \mu_S = \tan\theta. Rubber on asphalt (\mu \approx 0.9) holds up to about 42^\circ. A block that has just started sliding at that angle keeps sliding, because the smaller \mu_D then applies.

Common mistake — friction depends on the contact area

Tempting: a wide tyre or a brick lying flat has "more friction". In F_F = \mu F_N the area doesn't appear: spreading the same weight over a larger area lowers the pressure, and the two effects cancel. A brick needs the same push to slide on its large face as on its narrow side. The area does matter for air friction (section 4).

Common mistake — static friction is always \mu_S F_N

\mu_S F_N is a ceiling, not the actual value. In the crate example static friction is 100 N, not 147 N. Write F_F = \mu_S F_N only when the problem says the body is just about to slip.

Some friction values (board, "↳ coeff."):

Coefficient\mu_S\mu_D (gliding, sliding)
Steel on steel0.1 \ldots 0.50.04 \ldots 0.4
Rubber tire on asphalt\sim 0.9
Rubber tire on concrete\sim 1

(The board writes one value for the tyres, bracketed for both columns.) The braking example of 8 Newton's Laws and Forces needed \lvert a\rvert \approx 7\,\mathrm{m/s^2}. On a flat road the most the tyres can give is \mu F_N = \mu mg, so the largest braking deceleration is \mu g, the mass cancels. With \mu \approx 0.9 on dry asphalt that is about 8.8\,\mathrm{m/s^2}, so 7 is realistic; on ice it is much less.

3 A system with friction: block on a table and hanging block

Lecture: p. 9–10 ("Free-body diagrams" with friction, "continued") · Giancoli §5-1

The board redraws the system (sketch in section 1) and adds: on I, the friction force F_F (coloured) pointing left, against v and a (both to the right), and an arrow "m_1\cdot a_1" pointing left; on II, v and a pointing down and "m_2\cdot a_2" drawn upwards; axes x to the right, y up. "= CONTINUED …"

Now the block slides (the rope pulls it right, the hanging block falls), so there is sliding friction on I, pointing against the motion. The new "m \cdot a" arrows are inertial forces: d'Alembert's trick moves m\vec a to the other side of Newton's law,

\sum_i \vec F_i = m\,\vec a \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \sum_i \vec F_i - m\,\vec a = \vec 0
Symbols
  • \vec F_i — the forces on the body (N); m\vec a — its mass times acceleration; -m\vec a — the inertial force (N), drawn against the acceleration

and treats -m\vec a as an extra "force" pointing against the acceleration. Then every part looks as if it were in balance (\sum = 0) and can be written like statics. The inertial force is not a real force (no body exerts it), just like the centrifugal pseudo acceleration in 7 Rotational Kinematics and Circular Motion. That is why m_1 a_1 is drawn left (block 1 accelerates right) and m_2 a_2 up (block 2 accelerates down).

II (hanging block), with \downarrow F_{G2} and \uparrow m_2\cdot a_2 drawn above:

  • \sum F_x = 0, struck through: there are no horizontal forces on the hanging block at all;
  • \sum F_y = F_R - F_{G2} = m_2\cdot a_2 (circled, dashed underline), with \sum\vec F = m\vec a noted beside it;
  • boxed: \sum F_y = 0 = F_R - F_{G2} + m_2\cdot a_2 (up positive: rope +, weight -, inertial force +).

I (block on the table), boxed:

\sum F_x = F_R - F_{F1} - m_1\cdot a_1, \qquad \sum F_y = F_{N1} - F_{G1}, \qquad \boxed{\,F_{F1} = \mu_D\cdot F_{N1}\,}

Known: m_1, m_2, \mu_D; \quad a_1 = a_2 = a.

Symbols
  • F_R — rope force (N), the same at both blocks (ideal rope and pulley)
  • F_{G1} = m_1 g, F_{G2} = m_2 g — weights (N); F_{N1} — normal force of the table on block 1 (N)
  • F_{F1} — sliding friction on block 1 (N), pointing left
  • a_1, a_2 — the sizes of the accelerations of block 1 (to the right) and block 2 (downwards) (m/s²)
  • m_1 a_1, m_2 a_2 — the inertial forces (N), drawn against the accelerations

Horizontally on I (right positive): the rope pulls right (+F_R), friction left (-F_{F1}), the inertial force left (-m_1 a_1); the sum is meant to be 0. Vertically, F_{N1} up and F_{G1} down with no vertical motion, so F_{N1} = m_1 g. "a_1 = a_2 = a": the rope doesn't stretch, so whatever distance block 1 moves right, block 2 moves down. Count: unknowns F_R, F_{N1}, F_{F1}, a, four; equations II_y, I_x, I_y and the friction law, four. So the system can be solved; that is the "to be continued".

Unclear (p. 10): the first equation for II has the wrong sign

With y up and a_2 the size of the downward acceleration (as in the sketch), Newton's law in the usual form gives F_R - F_{G2} = -m_2 a_2. The circled line "F_R - F_{G2} = m_2\cdot a_2" would need a_2 to be the signed y-component (negative here). The boxed d'Alembert version 0 = F_R - F_{G2} + m_2 a_2 is consistent with the sketch; use that one. Also, the "= 0" in the boxed \sum F_x for I is implied, not written.

Continuing to the end (the board stops; the next lecture finishes it in 10 Torque, Gravitation, Work and Energy):

\begin{aligned} F_{N1} &= F_{G1} = m_1 g && \text{(I, } y\text{: no vertical motion)} \\ F_{F1} &= \mu_D\,m_1 g && \text{(friction law)} \\ F_R &= F_{F1} + m_1 a = \mu_D\,m_1 g + m_1 a && \text{(I, } x\text{: } 0 = F_R - F_{F1} - m_1 a) \\ F_R &= F_{G2} - m_2 a = m_2 g - m_2 a && \text{(II, } y\text{: } 0 = F_R - F_{G2} + m_2 a) \end{aligned}

Symbols as above. The rope force is the same in both, so set the right-hand sides equal and solve for a:

\begin{aligned} \mu_D\,m_1 g + m_1 a &= m_2 g - m_2 a && \text{(eliminate } F_R) \\ a &= \frac{(m_2 - \mu_D\,m_1)\,g}{m_1 + m_2} && \text{(}a \text{ terms left, factor, divide)} \\ F_R &= m_2\,(g - a) = \frac{m_1 m_2\,(1 + \mu_D)\,g}{m_1 + m_2} && \text{(back into II)} \end{aligned}

Symbols as above. Sanity checks: \mu_D = 0 gives a = \frac{m_2}{m_1 + m_2}\,g, the hanging weight accelerating both masses; m_1 \to 0 gives a \to g, block 2 just falls; and F_R < m_2 g whenever a > 0, as it must, since block 2 accelerates downwards.

Worked example — the system with numbers

m_1 = 4\,\mathrm{kg} on the table, m_2 = 2\,\mathrm{kg} hanging, \mu_D = 0.3.

  1. Friction: F_{N1} = 4 \cdot 9.81 = 39.24\,\mathrm N, F_{F1} = 0.3 \cdot 39.24 \approx 11.77\,\mathrm N.
  2. Acceleration: a = \dfrac{(2 - 0.3 \cdot 4) \cdot 9.81}{6} = \dfrac{0.8 \cdot 9.81}{6} \approx 1.31\,\mathrm{m/s^2}.
  3. Rope force: F_R = 2 \cdot (9.81 - 1.31) \approx 17.0\,\mathrm N, less than block 2's weight (19.6\,\mathrm N).
  4. Check with I: F_R - F_{F1} - m_1 a = 17.0 - 11.8 - 5.2 \approx 0 ✓.
  5. Does it start at all? Only if m_2 g beats the maximum static friction, m_2 > \mu_S m_1. If \mu_D m_1 > m_2, the formula gives a < 0: once pushed, the system would slow down and stop.
Common mistake — the rope force is not the hanging weight

Tempting: the rope "carries" block 2, so F_R = m_2 g. That is only true when nothing accelerates. If block 2 accelerates downwards, the net force on it must point down, so F_R < m_2 g (in the example 17.0\,\mathrm N instead of 19.6\,\mathrm N). Write the free-body diagram for each block and let the equations decide.

4 Speed-dependent friction: liquids and air

Lecture: p. 8 ("Liquid friction", "Air friction") · Giancoli §5-6

A body moving through a fluid (liquid or gas), or a fluid flowing through a pipe, feels a resistance that depends on the speed, unlike the contact friction of section 2.

Liquid friction (board: "→→ WATER IN A PIPE"):

F_F = C\cdot v

with "?" under C and "→ \rho_\text{liquid}, \nu", "GREEK LETTER 'NU'", VISCOSITY.

Symbols
  • F_F — friction force (N) for slow flow of a liquid, or a body moving slowly through one
  • C — a coefficient (marked "?"), depending on the liquid's density \rho_\text{liquid}, its viscosity \nu and the geometry; unit N/(m/s) = kg/s
  • v — flow speed (m/s)

Viscosity is the "thickness" of a fluid: honey has a much larger viscosity than water. In slow, smooth flow the fluid layers slide past each other, and the resistance grows in proportion to the speed.

Air friction:

F_{F,A} = C\cdot\rho_\text{AIR}\cdot A\cdot v^2

"COEFFICIENT ?" at C; "CONTACT AREA" at A; \rho_\text{AIR} \approx 1.2\ \mathrm{kg/m^3} at 1 atm \to \approx 1012\ \mathrm{mbar}.

Symbols
  • F_{F,A} — air friction (drag) force (N), opposite to the velocity
  • C — a coefficient (marked "?"), depending on the body's shape (dimensionless)
  • \rho_\text{air} — density of air (kg/m³) at normal pressure (1 atm ≈ 1013 mbar)
  • A — the "contact area": the cross-section facing the airflow (m²)
  • v — speed relative to the air (m/s)

C is dimensionless, since the rest already is a force:

[\rho\,A\,v^2] = \frac{\mathrm{kg}}{\mathrm{m^3}} \cdot \mathrm{m^2} \cdot \frac{\mathrm{m^2}}{\mathrm{s^2}} = \frac{\mathrm{kg\,m}}{\mathrm{s^2}} = \mathrm N

Symbols as above. It depends on the shape: a streamlined car has a small C, a flat plate a large one. Textbooks write the law as F = \tfrac12\,c_w\,\rho A v^2 with the drag coefficient c_w (\approx 0.3 for a modern car), so the board's C is \tfrac12 c_w. Why v^2: a body moving through air pushes the air in front of it out of the way; at twice the speed it pushes twice as much air per second and gives each bit twice the speed, so the force grows four times. A car with A = 2.2\,\mathrm{m^2}, c_w = 0.3: at 100\,\mathrm{km/h} (27.8\,\mathrm{m/s}) the drag is \tfrac12 \cdot 0.3 \cdot 1.2 \cdot 2.2 \cdot 27.8^2 \approx 306\,\mathrm N; at 130\,\mathrm{km/h} already \approx 516\,\mathrm N. "1 atm" is standard air pressure, about 1013 mbar (the board writes 1012); denser air gives more drag. Fast or turbulent liquid flow also behaves more like the v^2 law.

Beyond the lecture (Giancoli §5-6)

Because these forces grow with speed, a body falling through air or sinking in a liquid reaches a constant terminal velocity: friction grows until it equals the weight, the net force is zero, and the speed stops changing (axiom 1). For the v^2 law, mg = C\rho A v_T^2 gives v_T = \sqrt{mg/(C\rho A)}. This is why a feather falls slowly in air but not in vacuum (5 Uniformly Accelerated Motion and Free Fall).

5 Rolling friction and rope friction

Lecture: p. 8–9 · not in the downloaded Giancoli chapters

Rolling friction. Board sketch (p. 8–9): a wheel rolling with velocity v (turning, arrow) on the ground; "→ WHEEL ACCELERATING a \neq 0" and "→ a = 0"; the flattened contact patch at the bottom is circled.

F_F = \mu_W\cdot F_N
Symbols
  • F_F — rolling friction force (N), against the rolling motion
  • \mu_W — rolling friction coefficient (dimensionless), W for German Walzreibung
  • F_N — normal force on the wheel (N)

A rolling wheel doesn't slide (its contact point is momentarily at rest), so the loss isn't sliding friction. It comes from the wheel and the ground deforming at the flattened contact patch, the circle on the board, which costs far less. Typical values are tiny: about 0.01 for a car tyre on asphalt, about 0.001 for a steel train wheel on a rail, against \mu_D \approx 0.5–0.8 for a sliding tyre. That is why the wheel is such a good idea. The two labels a \neq 0 / a = 0 most likely mark that rolling friction acts whether the wheel speeds up or rolls steadily.

The board sums up: ⇒ STATIC FRICTION, SLIDING FRICTION, ROLLING FRICTION.

Rope friction.

F_{R1} > F_{R2}:

\boxed{\,F_{R1} = F_{R2}\cdot e^{\mu_R\,\alpha}\,} \qquad \alpha \text{ in RADIANS}
Symbols
  • F_{R1} — the larger rope force, on the side that is pulled (N)
  • F_{R2} — the smaller rope force, on the side that holds (N)
  • \mu_R — friction coefficient between rope and cylinder (dimensionless)
  • \alpha — the wrap angle over which the rope touches the cylinder, in radians (one full turn = 2\pi)
  • e \approx 2.718 — Euler's number
Where does the exponential come from?

Look at one tiny piece of the wrapped rope, covering the small angle \mathrm d\alpha, with tension F on one end and F + \mathrm dF on the other.

  1. How hard the piece presses on the cylinder: the tensions at its ends each point at the small angle \mathrm d\alpha/2 inwards from the tangent; their inward parts add up to 2F\sin(\mathrm d\alpha/2) \approx F\,\mathrm d\alpha (small angles, in rad). That is the normal force on the piece.
  2. Friction on the piece: \mu_R F\,\mathrm d\alpha, which is how much the tension can change across it: \mathrm dF = \mu_R\,F\,\mathrm d\alpha.
  3. Integrate from the holding end (F_{R2}) to the pulled end (F_{R1}), after dividing by F:
\int_{F_{R2}}^{F_{R1}} \frac{\mathrm dF}{F} = \int_0^{\alpha} \mu_R\,\mathrm d\alpha' \quad\Rightarrow\quad \ln\frac{F_{R1}}{F_{R2}} = \mu_R\,\alpha \quad\Rightarrow\quad F_{R1} = F_{R2}\,e^{\mu_R\alpha}

Symbols: \alpha' — integration variable (rad); \int \mathrm dF/F = \ln F.

Each extra bit of wrap multiplies the force ratio by the same factor: exponential growth. Step 1 used \sin x \approx x, valid only in radians, which is why the board insists on radians. This is often called the capstan or Euler–Eytelwein equation.

Worked example — three turns around a bollard

A rope with \mu_R = 0.3 is wound three times around a post. How much can a person hold with 10\,\mathrm N?

  1. Wrap angle in radians: \alpha = 3 \cdot 2\pi = 6\pi \approx 18.85.
  2. Exponent: \mu_R\alpha \approx 5.65, so e^{5.65} \approx 286.
  3. Force ratio: F_{R1} = 10\,\mathrm N \cdot 286 \approx 2.86\,\mathrm{kN}, the weight of about 290 kg.
  4. Compare: a quarter turn (\alpha = \pi/2) only gives e^{0.47} \approx 1.6; every extra full turn multiplies by e^{0.3 \cdot 2\pi} \approx 6.6.
Common mistake — degrees in the exponent

e^{\mu_R \alpha} needs \alpha in radians. Inserting 90 for a quarter turn gives e^{27}, an absurd factor of 5 \cdot 10^{11}, instead of \approx 1.6. Convert first (7 Rotational Kinematics and Circular Motion).
